item.text:
**Source map — OECD Economic Survey: Mexico 2022 (Chapter 2, extract pp. 102–127)**

*Source role:* International organisation (OECD), policy synthesis. Period coverage primarily 2017–2020, with some 2021 data; charter dated February 2022.

### Atomic claims (5B-relevant)

| # | Claim | Locator (page/fig/table) | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Digital government: 25% of Mexico's population used internet to interact with public authorities in 2019; Estonia rose from 50% (2009) to 80% (2019). | p.102 ¶1, citing OECD 2020 [61] | Observed fact (Mex.), international comparison |
| 2 | Digital diffusion lags: large education, age, and income gaps; only less than 30% of older adults (55–74) in Mexico use Internet vs. an OECD average of 60% (i.e. 60% OECD use vs <30% MX); wider internet-use divide related to age and educational attainment than in most other OECD countries. | p.103 ¶1, Figs.2.21–2.22 | Observed (ENDUTIH 2020; OECD DEO 2020) |
| 3 | Business digitalisation: ~9% of Mexican firms purchased cloud services vs ~32% OECD; share with web presence well below other OECD countries; IoT penetration "one of the lowest" among OECD; ~35% of firms accept digital payments, 57% in retail sector (ENAFIN 2018); online purchases below Chile/Brazil. | p.105 ¶2, Figs. 2.24–2.26 | Observed (ENAFIN 2018; OECD DEO 2020) |
| 4 | ICT task intensity of jobs "ranks low" in international comparison with "large regional disparities." | p.105 ¶3, Fig.2.27 (PIAAC 2018) | Observed |
| 5 | Digital payments: only one third of adults made ≥1 digital payment in 2017 vs almost two-thirds in Chile; 55% of credit-card holders used them in 2019 (CNBV 2020); cash used for 90% of small, 78% of large payments (ENIF 2018); regional concentrations in CDMX, Quintana Roo, Northern states. | p.108 ¶1, Fig.2.13 (ENIF 2018; CNBV 2020) | Observed |
| 6 | Payment-card market: five largest banks ≈80% share (Bátiz-Zuk & Lara Sánchez 2021); single domestic open system run by Asociación de Bancos de México; 4 clearing houses authorised — Prosa (Banorte, Santander, HSBC, Scotiabank), E-Global (BBVA, CITIBANAMEX), Visa Mexico, MasterCard Mexico (latter two not yet operational); also a closed credit-card system operated by American Express. Cross-system transaction rules and incumbent technical-approval requirement create barriers flagged by COFECE (2020). | p.109 ¶2, Box 2.5; p.110 ¶1 | Observed + interpretation; antitrust risk flagged by OECD/COFECE |
| 7 | Fintech Law (2018) slow authorisation: as of mid-October 2021, out of ~76 fintech firms demanding to operate in digital payments/crowdfunding, 17 fully authorised and 37 conditionally; online financial frauds = 70% of all financial frauds in Q1 2021. | p.110 ¶2 | Observed |
| 8 | CoDi (Banxico launch November 2019): only ~10% of fixed-broadband internet users know about it; ~2% have used it (IFT 2021); CoDi requires users (sellers and buyers) to hold a bank account and buyers need a 3G smartphone. | p.111 ¶1 | Observed |
| 9 | Identity: 89% of Mexican adults hold an identity document (Global Findex 2017), vs Costa Rica, Brazil and Peru (98%) or Chile (99%); RENAPO reports 0.8% of population lacks ID (INEGI 2015); 2020 government created a digital identity document and digital National Population Registry — "should be operative within the next two years." Identity system was fragmented with several institutions issuing different documents, no coordination mechanism to centralise information. | p.112 ¶1 | Observed + implementation claim (not yet realised) |
| 10 | CNBV digital onboarding: 2020 simplified regulation (extended to corporates and sociedades financieras populares); September 2021 extended digital on-boarding to remotely open accounts, sign contracts and validate transactions to brokerage houses, investment funds, small banks and other non-bank deposit-taking institutions and credit cooperatives. | p.112 ¶2 | Official reform (de jure) |
| 11 | Adult skills (PIAAC 2018): Mexico high-proficiency shares — Literacy 0.8%, Numeracy 0.7%, Problem Solving 10%; OECD means 10/11/30%; ~39% of Mexican adults lack very basic computer skills; less than 1% achieve high proficiency in numeracy and literacy and 10% in problem solving (Table 2.1 / Box 2.8). | p.114, Table 2.1, Box 2.8 | Observed |
| 12 | Regional cognitive-skill gap: CDMX & Northern states best; numeracy and literacy present the largest regional gaps (Fig. 2.29); informal workers have lower cognitive skills than formal workers (Fig. 2.30); among trained informal workers slightly more than half received employer funding vs 85% of formal workers. | p.115, Figs. 2.29–2.30 | Observed |
| 13 | Digital skills programmes: MexicoX (over 230 courses for specialised/academic teacher training, more than 1.5 million users); @prende.mx (schools, technological equipment, teacher knowledge-sharing platforms, student pilots) — "An assessment on the effectiveness of these policies on broader education outcomes or skills development would be useful." | p.115 ¶2 | Author assertion (un-evaluated) |
| 14 | Policy recommendations (selected, from Table 2.2): strengthen credit registry; alternative-source credit scoring for informal firms; specialised commercial courts and courts infrastructure; simplify SME stock-market requirements; promote alternative digital data for credit assessment (utilities/loan payments, government data); increase social-programme delivery through bank accounts; consumer-protection awareness; financial-education reform focused on low-income adults; upgrade digital payment regulation; eliminate uncertainty in cross-system secondary regulation; impartiality in incumbent clearing-house approval; modify school curriculum for digital literacy and upskill teachers; monitor/upgrade regulatory-sandbox regulation; increase fixed-broadband competition; cash-rebates/lotteries/consumer rewards for digital payments; monitor/increase funding for micro/SME online-selling programmes. | p.116–117, Table 2.2 | OECD recommendations, not enacted |

### Key qualifications preserved
- All digital-divide and payments data are **national statistics / surveys** (ENDUTIH, ENIF, ENAFIN, CNBV) **not** OECD modelling.
- Recommendations in Table 2.2 are **proposals**, not policy enacted by the AMLO administration.
- 2020 digital-ID measure and digital National Population Registry are **announced**, "not yet operative" — treat as **author assertion of intent**, not realisation.
- CoDi usage numbers (IFT 2021) describe **awareness/use among fixed-broadband internet users**, not population-wide.
- Period anchor: data mostly 2017–2020; some 2021 (CoDi survey, fraud stats); no later reforms discussed.
- South Korea is also referenced alongside Estonia as a digital-government success case (UN e-government development index; political commitment, ICT infrastructure, national digital identification system).

### Limitations / contrary material / reopen notes
- Extract focuses on **digital/finance access (Chapter 2 / Special Feature)**, not the macroeconomic pillar (fiscal/debt/inflation — 5B.3) or competition/regulation (5B.4) sections; reopened chapters needed for those 5B questions.
- No primary government or Ministry of Finance text cited; revenue/capacity claims absent from this slice.
- MexicoX/@prende.mx "effectiveness … would be useful to assess" — OECD flags the gap, claim not adopted as effective.
- Fintech authorisations: denominator ~76 mid-October 2021; status of conditional approvals after that date **unknown** in extract.
- "Mexico ranks last in the development of Internet of Things technology" (Fig.2.25 title) is stated as "last" by the OECD — phrasing should be retained with the OECD's own caveat that the figure depicts OECD comparators.
- Author/institutional incentives not inferred beyond OECD's stated oversight mandate (Box 2.7 principles).
- The 2018 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC 2018) is the source for the high-proficiency shares cited in Table 2.1 / Box 2.8; the figure titles state "literacy, numeracy and problem solving" — problem-solving for Mexico is 10%, and "less than 1%" is stated for combined high proficiency in numeracy and literacy.

### 5B question coverage (this extract)
- **5B.6** infrastructure/admin capacity/regulation: strong coverage (digital govt, broadband, fintech reg, courts, ID, payment card regulation).
- **5B.7** information, audit, correction: partial (PIAAC, ENIF/ENAFIN data, but no audit-institution review).
- **5B.8** distributional findings: rich (region, age, education, formal/informal, gender via "kinship tax" cited literature).
- **5B.9** shock response: pandemic-accelerated digitalisation and digital-onboarding; confinement triggered shift to online purchases/digital payments.
- **5B.10** durable trajectory: implicit (skills agenda, digital identity pipeline, open-finance data sharing), not explicit forecast.
- **5B.3 / 5B.4 / 5B.5:** outside this chunk; reopen with fiscal/chapter-1 and competition sections.

*Continuation flag:* Macro/competition chapters (5B.3, 5B.4, 5B.5) require separate OECD Survey chunk ingestion before chapter judgement.
